::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 14) you can:

1. **model** temporal graphs as snapshots or event streams and explain TGN's
   memory / message / embedding loop at architecture level;
2. **derive** LightGCN from Week 6's GCN — justifying each deletion — and
   train it with BPR; tell the PinSage web-scale story accurately;
3. **evaluate** a recommender properly: Recall@K and NDCG@K computed by hand,
   and a split that respects time — with the measured cost of not doing so;
4. **explain** Relational Deep Learning: a company database as a temporal
   heterogeneous graph, and why RelBench threatens hand-built feature
   pipelines;
5. **place** GraphRAG, fraud detection, and your own project on the
   production map of graph ML.
:::

## A Thursday at a marketplace company

Picture the company this course has been secretly preparing you for: a
marketplace — buyers, sellers, listings, payments, messages. Walk its
machine-learning floor on a Thursday morning. One team ships the
recommendation feed: a bipartite graph of users and items, a hundred
million interactions a day, embeddings served in milliseconds. Two desks
over, the integrity team hunts fraud rings: a heterogeneous graph of
accounts, devices, cards, and addresses — Week 10's typed machinery with
an adversary on the other side.

Down the hall, the analytics-ML group is
quietly replacing five years of hand-built features with a model that
reads the company's *database itself* as a graph. And the newest hire is
wiring the support chatbot to a knowledge graph so it stops inventing
refund policies — Week 5, employed.

Nothing in this picture is hypothetical: it is a composite of the job
postings this course's final section will map, and the four desks
disagree about almost everything — architectures, latencies, failure
costs — except the discipline this lecture teaches.

Four teams, four systems, one syllabus. Everything on that floor is
machinery you now own: message passing, embeddings, negative sampling,
sampling at scale, split discipline. What none of our previous weeks
supplied — and what every desk on that floor fights daily — is **time**.
Interactions arrive as a stream, not a matrix. The graph you trained on
is stale by lunch. And the evaluation question stops being "how well does
the model score on held-out edges" and becomes the only question
production ever asks: *how well does what I trained on the past predict
the future?* This week is about what time does to graph ML — to the
models (a memory), to the training (an ordering), and above all to the
evaluation (a wall). It is the last lecture of new machinery in this
course, and it ends, fittingly, with a map of where all of it goes to
work.

One framing sentence to carry through: **production graph ML is this
course's models under this course's discipline, with the clock as a new
adversary.** The models will turn out to be *simpler* than what you
built in Weeks 10–13 — the star of today's measured section deletes
almost everything from GCN. The discipline gets *harder*, because time
gives leakage a thousand new doors. Simple models, strict protocols:
that inversion is the single most reliable description of the field's
production reality, and by the end of the lecture you will have measured
exactly why it holds.

## Time enters the graph

A graph, so far, has been a fact: $G = (V, E)$, frozen. Production
graphs are histories, and the object deserves a formal name, because
everything in this lecture is a consequence of it.

::: {#def-w14-stream .definition name="Temporal event stream"}
A **temporal event stream** is a time-ordered sequence of events
$(u, v, t, \mathbf{x})$: an edge between nodes $u$ and $v$, stamped
with time $t$, carrying optional features $\mathbf{x}$ — arriving
forever, with no final state. Read every "the graph" in this
lecture as shorthand for *the stream accumulated up to some moment*.
:::

Two modeling stances exist for such an object, and the choice between
them is the first design decision of any temporal system.

**Snapshots** (discrete time): slice the stream into windows — the graph
as of each day, each hour — and run any static GNN per slice, optionally
with a sequence model (an RNN, a transformer) stitched across slices.
Cheap, compatible with everything you know, and *lossy in exactly one
way*: within a window, order disappears. If an account receives money
and forwards it away within one window, the snapshot shows a node with
one in-edge and one out-edge — the *sequence*, which is the entire fraud
signal, is gone. Snapshots are the right answer when the phenomenon's
natural timescale is slower than your window, and quietly wrong
otherwise.

**Event streams** (continuous time): consume the events one by one, in
order, and maintain per-node *state*. This is the stance of the temporal
graph network family, TGN
([Rossi et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10637)), and its
architecture is worth holding as one loop:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w14-tgn.html >}}

Every event $(u, v, t)$ generates a **message** for each endpoint — a
function of the two nodes' current states, the time gap since each was
last seen, and the event's features — and the message updates each
endpoint's **memory** through a recurrent cell:

$$m_u = \mathrm{msg}\big(s_u, s_v, \Delta t_u, \mathbf{x}\big),
\qquad
s_u \leftarrow \mathrm{GRU}\big(s_u, m_u\big),$$ {#eq-w14-tgn}

where —

- $s_u, s_v$ are the endpoints' **memories** — one state vector per
  node, initialized to zero and persisting across events;
- $\Delta t_u$ is the time elapsed since $u$ was last seen ($v$ gets its
  own message with $\Delta t_v$, symmetrically);
- $\mathbf{x}$ is the event's feature vector;
- $\mathrm{msg}$ is the message function — in practice a concatenation
  or a small learned network;
- $\mathrm{GRU}$ is a gated recurrent unit: a small recurrent cell that
  mixes old state with new input through learned gates.

When a prediction is needed, an **embedding module** — typically one or
two layers of attention over recent temporal neighbors — computes a
fresh, time-aware representation from the memory:

$$h_u(t) = \mathrm{Embed}\big(s_u,\;
\{(v, t', \mathbf{x}') : t' < t\}\big),$$ {#eq-w14-tgn-embed}

where $h_u(t)$ is $u$'s representation *as of query time $t$*, and the
second argument is $u$'s recent temporal neighborhood — the events
(neighbor $v$, stamp $t'$, features $\mathbf{x}'$) involving $u$ that
happened strictly *before* $t$. The module exists to correct for
staleness: a node last seen hours ago should not be represented as if
its memory were current, and the time-difference input lets the model
learn exactly how to decay its confidence. Memory carries the deep past
cheaply; the embedding layer reads the recent past sharply; the
division of labor is the architecture.

Three consequences deserve engraving. First, **inference is a stream
too**: the deployed model updates memories as events arrive — the model
you serve at noon is not the model you served at nine, by design.
Second, **training must respect the arrow**: batches are consecutive
slices of the event stream, each processed with memories as they stood
*before* it — shuffle the events like i.i.d. samples and you have built
a machine that reads the future, which is this lecture's evaluation sin
committed inside the forward pass. Third, the **temporal neighbor
sampler** — "give me this node's last 20 interactions before time $t$" —
is Week 11's sampling machinery with a timestamp filter, and building it
wrong (allowing neighbors *after* $t$) is the single most common
implementation bug in the genre. Lab 14's stretch has you feel it.

The training subtlety deserves one more level of detail, because it is
where every first implementation goes wrong and where the published
architecture is genuinely clever. Within a training batch, the naive
order of operations — update memories with the batch's events, then
predict the batch's events — lets each prediction read a memory that
already contains the event being predicted: self-leakage, one event
wide.

TGN's fix is a **raw message store**: events update memories one
batch *late*, so a batch is always predicted from state that predates
it, and the gradient still reaches the memory functions through the
delayed update. It is Week 12's leak taxonomy in miniature — the
information that must not flow is not "the future" loosely, but *this
exact edge* — and the fix is the same shape as SEAL's: remove the
target from what the model conditions on. When you audit any temporal
model, this is the first question: *at the moment of predicting event
$e$, prove to me the state excludes $e$.*

The pieces assemble into one loop — the formal statement of what the
figure schematizes.

::: {#alg-w14-tgn .algorithm name="TGN Event Processing"}
One pass over a batch of consecutive events: predict each event from
state that predates it, then let the batch update the memories.

**Input:** event stream $(u, v, t, \mathbf{x})$ in time order, cut into
consecutive batches; memories $s$ (all zeros at start); message function
$\mathrm{msg}$; $\mathrm{GRU}$; embedding module $\mathrm{Embed}$.
**Output:** one prediction per event; updated memories $s$.

1. **for** each batch of consecutive events **do**
2. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;apply the *previous* batch's stored messages to $s$ (@eq-w14-tgn)
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each event $(u, v, t, \mathbf{x})$ in the batch **do**
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$h_u(t), h_v(t) \leftarrow$ time-aware embeddings (@eq-w14-tgn-embed)
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;predict the event from $h_u(t), h_v(t)$; accumulate the loss
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;store raw messages $m_u, m_v$ for the *next* flush
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;gradient step (credit reaches $\mathrm{msg}$ and the GRU through step 2)
9. **end for**
:::

Step 2 is the raw-message-store subtlety in one line — the answer to
the auditor's "prove the state excludes $e$" — and step 4's
strictly-before filter is the one-character bug from the pitfall list.
Cost per event is constant in the graph's size, which is what
makes the stream stance servable. This float stays lecture-side: Lab
14's stretch builds the memory line, not the full loop.

Also worth naming, because interviews love it: the stream stance
handles **deletions and updates** naturally (an unfriend, a refund, a
price change is just another event updating memory), while snapshots
must re-materialize; and conversely, snapshots parallelize trivially
(every slice is an independent static-GNN job — Week 11's cheapest kind
of scale) while streams serialize on the memory. Neither stance
dominates; the timescale of the phenomenon decides, and mature systems
often run both — a stream model for the fast signals riding on
snapshot-refreshed base embeddings.

That is TGN at architecture level — the level this course needs, because
the deeper lesson is not the GRU's equations but the shape: *state per
node, updated by events, read out on demand*. You will meet the shape
again in the fraud section, in RDL's temporal tables, and in any system
whose graph will not sit still.

## The recommender: a graph problem wearing a product

Now to the floor's biggest desk. Recommendation is, by a wide margin,
graph ML's largest production deployment, and its core object could not
be more familiar: a **bipartite graph**, users on one side, items on the
other, an edge per interaction. Our laboratory this week is the classic
MovieLens-100k: 943 users, 1,682 movies, exactly 100,000 timestamped
ratings spanning seven months of 1997–98 — about 106 interactions per
user, a density of 6.3%. Laughably small by industry standards, and
precisely right for the course's method: small enough to train a full
ladder in a minute, real enough for every protocol lesson to transfer
unchanged.

Start from what Week 3 would do: give every user and every item a
learned embedding, and score a pair by the dot product

$$\hat{y}_{ui} = e_u \cdot e_i,$$ {#eq-w14-mf}

where —

- $e_u, e_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are user $u$'s and item $i$'s embeddings —
  free parameters, one row per ID;
- $\hat{y}_{ui}$ is the predicted affinity, the number by which each
  user's item list is ranked;

and train the embeddings so observed interactions score high. That is
**matrix factorization** (MF), the recommender workhorse of two
decades and the engine of the Netflix Prize era, and note carefully
what it is in this course's vocabulary: a *zero-layer* GNN — embeddings straight to
scores, the graph consulted only to say which pairs are positive. The
co-consumption structure — users who share items, items that share
users — never touches the model's forward pass.

Week 6 taught the machine that would use it: message passing over the
interaction graph. So run the obvious experiment — put a GCN on the
bipartite graph. The field did, with enthusiasm: the late-2010s
produced increasingly ornate neural recommenders, GCN variants with
gated interactions and attention flourishes stacked on the bipartite
graph.

Then came one of the field's healthiest papers, whose
contribution was *deletions*: the LightGCN authors
([He et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02126)) took the reigning
graph recommender, removed its pieces one ablation at a time, and
found that accuracy went **up** with each removal — the feature
transforms and nonlinearities were not merely dead weight but actively
in the way, complicating optimization on a problem whose inputs carry
no feature structure to transform. It is the cleanest published
instance of a pattern this course has now measured three times
(Week 10's lookup beating the R-GCN encoder; Week 13's attention
buying nothing at matched budget): *capacity that the task cannot use
is not neutral — it costs optimization, and honest ablations find
this*.

On interaction graphs with no features but IDs, most of the GCN
is dead weight, and here is why each piece falls. The feature transform
$W$? There are no feature axes to remix — every input is a free
embedding that training can pre-rotate however it likes; a $W$ can only
re-parameterize what the embeddings already express. The nonlinearity?
Between two averaging steps it mostly discards sign information that
dot-product scoring needs. The self-loop? Replaced by something better,
as you will see. Delete all three and what survives is **LightGCN**:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w14-lightgcn.html >}}

Propagation only:

$$e_u^{(k+1)} = \sum_{i \in N(u)} \frac{e_i^{(k)}}{\sqrt{d_u d_i}},
\qquad
e_i^{(k+1)} = \sum_{u \in N(i)} \frac{e_u^{(k)}}{\sqrt{d_u d_i}},$$ {#eq-w14-lightgcn}

where —

- $e_u^{(k)}, e_i^{(k)}$ are user $u$'s and item $i$'s embeddings after
  $k$ propagation rounds, $e^{(0)}$ being the learned tables of
  @eq-w14-mf themselves;
- $N(u)$ is the set of items $u$ interacted with, $N(i)$ the set of
  users who interacted with $i$ — neighborhoods in the bipartite graph;
- $d_u = |N(u)|$ and $d_i = |N(i)|$ are their degrees, making
  $1/\sqrt{d_u d_i}$ Week 6's symmetric normalization;
- $K$, the **depth**, is the number of propagation rounds — the model's
  only architectural knob, and the $K$ of the measured ladder below.

@eq-w14-lightgcn is followed by the one non-obvious design choice, the
**layer-mean readout**: the final embedding is the average of *all*
layers,

$$e = \frac{1}{K+1}\sum_{k=0}^{K} e^{(k)},$$ {#eq-w14-readout}

where the mean runs over all depths $k = 0 \dots K$, each weighted
equally. This is why the self-loop
could go — the mean keeps every node's own signal (the $k{=}0$ term) in
the final answer at full strength while the propagated terms add
neighborhood context, and it simultaneously tempers Week 7's
oversmoothing: deep layers contribute, but diluted by the average
rather than compounding.

Drive the propagation yourself before believing anything about it:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w14-propagate.html >}}

The widget is the argument for the whole architecture. At $K{=}0$, u1's
signal reaches no other user: plain MF, every user an island connected
only to its own items. At $K{=}2$, the **co-consumption hop** arrives —
u2 holds mass 0.250 of u1's signal, received *entirely* through the
shared item i2 — and this is the exact information MF structurally
cannot receive: "users like you liked…" as a term in the forward pass
rather than a slogan on a slide. At $K{=}4$ even the stranger u3 hears a
whisper (0.063, via u2's items). Collaborative filtering's folk wisdom,
recast as Week 6 mathematics: *similar users* means *short even-length
paths in the bipartite graph*, and propagation depth is the radius of
"similar."

One proposition makes the connection to this course's spine exact, and
it is worth stating formally because it explains both LightGCN's speed
and its limits.

::: {.proposition #prp-w14-sgc}
LightGCN's encoder is linear in its parameters: with $E^{(0)}$ the
stacked user–item embedding matrix and $\hat A$ the symmetrically
normalized bipartite adjacency, the final embeddings are
$E = \frac{1}{K+1}\sum_{k=0}^{K} \hat A^{k} E^{(0)}$ — a fixed
polynomial in $\hat A$ applied to the only learnable object, $E^{(0)}$.
LightGCN is SGC (Week 11) with identity features: all depth is
precomputable structure, and the "network" trains nothing but the
lookup table.
:::

The proof is the definition read twice: no $W$, no nonlinearity, so the
layer map is multiplication by $\hat A$, and compositions of linear maps
collapse. Week 11's consequences transfer wholesale — the polynomial
$\frac{1}{K+1}\sum_k \hat A^k$ can be applied once, offline, making
industrial serving a dot product against precomputed vectors — and so
does the ceiling: whatever a fixed linear filter cannot express, no
amount of LightGCN training recovers. Week 6's spectral eyes add the
final reading: $\frac{1}{K+1}\sum_k \hat A^k$ is a low-pass filter on
the interaction graph — it amplifies embedding components that vary
smoothly across co-consumption neighborhoods and shrinks the jagged
ones, with the layer-mean's coefficients $(1, 1, \dots, 1)/(K{+}1)$
giving a gentler roll-off than $\hat A^K$ alone (which is why the mean
oversmooths less than the last layer would). "Collaborative filtering"
turns out to be literal: the collaboration is the graph, and the
filtering is Week 6's, applied to a learned signal. The recommender that dominates
production is, in this course's terms, the *simplest model of Week 11*
pointed at the *simplest graph of Week 1*. Simple models, strict
protocols.

Before the loss, one structural caution that the propagation equations
carry quietly. Averaging over neighborhoods gives high-degree items
gravitational pull: a bestseller sits in millions of user
neighborhoods, so every propagation layer spreads its embedding wider
and pulls user vectors toward it — **popularity bias, amplified by the
very mechanism that makes the model work**. The $1/\sqrt{d_u d_i}$
normalization is the counterweight (a hub's outgoing influence is
discounted by its own degree — Week 6's normalization debate, now with
a business consequence), and it is only partial: production systems add
explicit popularity corrections in sampling, in the loss, or
post-ranking, because a feed that converges to "everyone gets the
bestseller list" is a feed that no longer needs its model — and worse,
its *logs* then teach the next model the same lesson. The feedback
loop is real, it compounds quarterly, and the popularity baseline you
are about to see embarrass MF is also the attractor the whole system
drifts toward when nobody prices this bias.

And its mirror image: **cold start**. A brand-new user or item has no
edges, so every mechanism in this section — propagation, BPR, the dot
product itself — has literally nothing to grip; an ID embedding with no
interactions is a random vector. Production's answers come from
outside the interaction graph: content features (a *two-tower* encoder
maps item text and images, and user context, into the same space, so
new items land near their kin by content alone), onboarding
questionnaires, and popularity fallbacks while the first edges accrue.
Remember this when our temporal wall discards 877 of 943 users as
unevaluable: the discard is the honest protocol's way of *pointing at*
the cold-start subproblem, not a license to forget it exists.

**Training: BPR.** What loss? Week 4 already taught it, under another
name. Observed interactions are positives; everything unobserved is not
a negative but an *unknown* — the user has not seen most items, and
"unseen" must not be taught as "disliked." The escape is to train on
*pairs*, the move [Rendle et al., 2009](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.2618)
named Bayesian Personalized Ranking.

::: {#def-w14-bpr .definition name="Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR)"}
For a user $u$, an observed item $i$, and a sampled unobserved item
$j$, **BPR** asks only that the observed item score higher than the
sampled one. Read it as a ranking statement, never a labeling one.
:::

The loss, per sampled triple $(u, i, j)$:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma\!\big(e_u \cdot e_i - e_u \cdot e_j\big)
+ \lambda \lVert \Theta \rVert^2 ,$$ {#eq-w14-bpr}

where —

- $e_u, e_i, e_j$ are the user's, the observed item's, and the sampled
  item's final embeddings, scored by @eq-w14-mf's dot product;
- $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid $\sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})$ —
  squashing the score difference into "the probability the ordering is
  right";
- $\Theta$ collects every trainable parameter — for LightGCN, nothing
  but the embedding tables — and $\lambda$ sets the strength of the L2
  penalty on them.

Why pairs and not labels? Because the tempting pointwise alternative —
binary cross-entropy with observed = 1, unobserved = 0 — teaches the
model a falsehood at scale: it spends most of its gradient pushing
scores of *never-shown* items toward zero, including precisely the
items the user would love, which are the ones the system exists to
find. BPR's pairwise form only ever asserts the comparison actually
supported by the data — "this user chose $i$ while $j$ sat unchosen" —
and its gradient makes the mechanics vivid: writing
$x_{uij} = e_u \cdot e_i - e_u \cdot e_j$ for the score difference
inside @eq-w14-bpr's sigmoid, the update is proportional to
$\sigma(-x_{uij})$, the model's *disbelief* in the correct ordering,
so confidently-ranked pairs teach nothing and each step spends itself
on the violations.

Read that twice and you will recognize Week 4's
TransE session: push the positive pair up, the sampled negative down,
learn from ranking violations rather than absolute labels. Ranking
losses, negative sampling, the same worries (popular items get sampled
as negatives too often, so production samplers correct toward
popularity; hard negatives help until they poison — a near-duplicate
of the watched item is a *false* negative) — the KG embedding toolbox
transfers to recommenders nearly verbatim, because both problems are
"score the true edge above the fake one" at heart. One course, one
loss family, two industries.

Model and loss now assemble into the training loop Lab 14 has you
build as `propagate` and `bpr_loss` — He et al.'s recipe in full:

::: {#alg-w14-lightgcn .algorithm name="LightGCN with BPR"}
One training epoch: propagate the embedding tables through the
interaction graph, sample a negative per observed pair, take a BPR step.

**Input:** train interactions $T$; normalized bipartite operators
$\hat A_{ui}, \hat A_{iu}$ (@eq-w14-lightgcn's sums, as matrices);
depth $K$; embedding tables $P^{(0)}$ (users), $Q^{(0)}$ (items);
L2 strength $\lambda$.
**Output:** trained $P^{(0)}, Q^{(0)}$; final embeddings $P, Q$.

1. **for** each batch of observed pairs $(u, i) \subset T$ **do**
2. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;sample one unobserved item $j$ per pair
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** $k = 1 \dots K$ **do**
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$P^{(k)} \leftarrow \hat A_{ui}\, Q^{(k-1)}$; &nbsp;$Q^{(k)} \leftarrow \hat A_{iu}\, P^{(k-1)}$
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$P \leftarrow \mathrm{mean}\big(P^{(0)}, \dots, P^{(K)}\big)$; likewise $Q$ (@eq-w14-readout)
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\ell \leftarrow -\mathrm{mean}\,\log\sigma\big(P_u \cdot (Q_i - Q_j)\big) + \lambda\lVert\Theta\rVert^2$
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;gradient step on $\ell$ — the only parameters are $P^{(0)}, Q^{(0)}$
9. **end for**
10. **return** $P, Q$ — serve by ranking $P_u \cdot Q_i$, train items masked
:::

Step 4 is the lab's flagged trap: both updates read the *previous*
layer's pair — compute $P^{(k)}$ from $Q^{(k-1)}$, never from the
just-updated $Q^{(k)}$. Step 8 restates @prp-w14-sgc: the propagation
is a fixed linear map, so every gradient lands on the embedding tables
— depth trains nothing. Cost per batch: $K$ sparse multiplies,
$O(K\,|E|\,d)$; epochs repeat the loop with early stopping on
validation Recall@20, as Lab 14's harness does.

**And the web-scale coda: PinSage.** The story every practitioner should
be able to tell in four sentences. Pinterest, 2018
([Ying et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01973)): three billion
nodes, eighteen billion edges — the first GNN at genuinely industrial
scale, years before the tooling made that routine.

The architecture was Week 7's GraphSAGE
([Hamilton et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02216)); the
achievement was Week 11's chapter executed at full
force: neighborhoods defined not by adjacency but by **random-walk
importance** (visit counts from short walks — Week 2's PageRank
intuition drafted into sampling), aggregation weighted by those counts,
training with a curriculum of progressively harder negatives (Week 4's
lesson, industrialized), and inference run as a giant MapReduce sweep so
that every node's embedding is computed exactly once per layer.
Nothing in PinSage is a new idea by Week 14 of this course — and that is
the point worth saying out loud: at scale, the innovations are
*systems*, and the model is deliberately boring.

Which raises the question the papers rarely spell out: what does
*serving* a recommender actually look like? The proposition below
supplies the answer's first half — LightGCN's graph work can be done
offline, leaving each user and item a fixed vector. The second half is
one of applied ML's great workhorse tricks: with scores that are dot
products, "find this user's top $K$ items" is a **maximum inner
product search**, and approximate nearest-neighbor indexes answer it
in sub-millisecond time over hundreds of millions of items — the
difference between a ranking model and a ranking *product* is largely
this index.

Hence the canonical two-stage shape of every large feed:
a cheap embedding **retrieval** stage narrows a hundred million
candidates to a few hundred (this lecture's models live here), then a
heavy **ranker** — often a plain gradient-boosted or deep tabular
model stuffed with features, including graph-derived ones — orders the
survivors with the expensive context (freshness, diversity, business
rules) that dot products cannot carry. When the map at the end of this
lecture says "recommendation employs the most graph ML," it mostly
means that retrieval stage: embeddings from a bipartite graph, served
from an ANN index, refreshed on a schedule whose staleness someone has
consciously priced.

## Grading a ranker: two numbers, computed on a napkin

Before any measurement can be honest, the metric has to be understood at
the fingertip level. A recommender's output is a *ranking* — for each
user, all items they have not yet interacted with, ordered by score —
and ranking metrics have a small anatomy that fits in one widget. One
notational warning first: the $K$ in Recall@K is the **ranking
cutoff** — how far down the list the metric looks — and has nothing to
do with the $K$ that counted propagation depth two sections ago. The
letter works both jobs across the literature; this lecture says
"depth" for the architectural one and pins the cutoff at 20.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w14-metrics.html >}}

::: {#def-w14-metrics .definition name="Recall@K and NDCG@K"}
For one user, let $R_K$ be the model's top-$K$ ranked items (training
items masked out) and $P$ the user's held-out positives. Then

$$\mathrm{Recall@}K = \frac{|R_K \cap P|}{\min(|P|,\, K)},
\qquad
\mathrm{NDCG@}K = \frac{1}{\mathrm{IDCG}@K}
\sum_{\substack{r \le K \\ \text{hit at rank } r}} \frac{1}{\log_2(r+1)},$$ {#eq-w14-metrics}

each averaged over evaluable users. Recall grades *coverage* — what
fraction of the true items the window caught; NDCG grades *placement*
too, paying each hit by its rank.
:::

where —

- $K$ is the ranking cutoff — the window size, *not* propagation depth;
- $P$ is the held-out positive set; the $\min(|P|, K)$ cap keeps a user
  with thirty positives from being "failed" by a twenty-slot window;
- $r$ is a hit's rank, discounted by $1/\log_2(r+1)$ — the widget
  walks the values;
- $\mathrm{IDCG}@K$ is the same discounted sum for the best achievable
  arrangement (all positives packed at the top), so NDCG $= 1.0$ means
  "everything found *and* front-loaded."

Drive
the widget's $K$ to 10 and read the disagreement: recall reaches 1.000
(everything found) while NDCG sits at 0.813, still charging for the hit
that arrived at rank 9. Coverage versus placement; a feed with
eight slots cares desperately about the difference.

You have run this metric family before, under other names. Week 4's KG
completion graded rankings with MRR and Hits@K, and its *filtered*
protocol — remove the already-known true triples from the candidate
list before ranking — reappears here as masking the user's training
items from the ranked list, same move, same justification: don't
penalize the model for ranking highly something we *told* it. The
recommender twist is the **candidate set**: ranking against all 1,682
items (our protocol) and ranking against 100 sampled candidates are
different examinations wearing the same metric's name, and the sampled
one is dramatically easier — mid-2020s audits showed sampled metrics
can invert system orderings outright. A reported Recall@20 without its
candidate-set sentence is a number wearing no units.

Both metrics come with a habit worth automating: **always compute the
popularity baseline.** Rank every user the same global bestseller list
and score it. It costs one line, and this lecture's measured section is
about to show you why skipping that line has embarrassed more than one
published table.

## The split is the experiment

Here is the week's centerpiece, and the course's oldest lesson wearing
its production uniform. We trained the *same* LightGCN ($K{=}3$,
$d{=}64$, BPR, seed 0) on the *same* 100,000 interactions under three
evaluation protocols, and the three numbers it returned are not three
estimates of one quantity — they are three different quantities:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w14-splits.html >}}

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** The random split scored 0.346. Before
reading on: *why* is that number a lie for a deployed recommender? Name
the mechanism — what exactly does the model see at training time that
deployment will never grant it?

::: {.predict-answer}
Under a random split, 20% of interactions are hidden uniformly across
the timeline — so for a typical user, the model trains on interactions
from *after* the ones it is tested on. It learns from March to
"predict" January. Deployment only ever runs the other direction: train
on everything up to now, predict what has not happened yet. The random
number measures interpolation into a known past; the deployed system
performs extrapolation into an unknown future; measured on the same
model, the gap between those two tasks is a factor of 1.77.
:::
:::

Walk the timeline yourself — one user, three protocols, and the moment
the absurdity clicks is the moment this section is over:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w14-splits.html >}}

The first protocol is deployment's actual contract, and it earns the
formal statement.

::: {#def-w14-wall .definition name="Global temporal split"}
Fix a wall time $t^{\ast}$ — here the 80% quantile of all timestamps
(for our seven months of data, March 7, 1998). Train on interactions
strictly before $t^{\ast}$; evaluate only on interactions after it
(validation and test partitioned by a second wall). One line certifies
the whole contract: $\max(\text{train timestamps}) \le
\min(\text{test timestamps})$ — the no-leakage guarantee, *checkable
by machine*.
:::

That auditing convenience makes the split Lab 14's exercise 1: one
assert, where fancier schemes take a page of argument. Protocols you
can assert beat protocols you can only defend.
The wall is also brutally
honest about a cost the other protocols hide: of 943 users, only **66**
have test interactions that the wall permits evaluating (the rest went
quiet, or are new-and-unseen — cold start, of which more below). A
thin, awkward, honest evaluation population.

**Leave-last-out** — hold
out each user's final interaction — is the literature's usual
compromise: 940 evaluable users, per-user time respected, but global
time scrambled (user A's held-out "future" may predate user B's
training "past", so item popularity statistics still leak across the
wall). And the **random split** is the protocol Week 12 taught you to
refuse, now with a recommender-shaped price tag: **0.346 versus 0.195,
a ×1.77 inflation, from the split alone.** Nothing about the model
changed. Nothing about the data changed. The number nearly doubled.

If you keep one sentence from this lecture, keep the figure's caption:
*the metric is a property of the model AND the protocol, and quoting
one without the other is not a result — it is an advertisement.*

## The measured ladder, honestly read

With the honest protocol fixed, the architecture question becomes
answerable: what does each propagation layer actually buy? The
protocol card first, as always: MovieLens-100k, all 100,000
interactions as implicit positives; global temporal 80/10/10; LightGCN
$d = 64$, BPR with uniform negatives, Adam, early stopping on
validation Recall@20 checked every 20 epochs; one seed; popularity
baseline included because the previous section said so. Test Recall@20,
best-validation checkpoint:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w14-ladder.html >}}

Read it with the widget-1 story in hand. **Popularity scores 0.1655 —
and beats matrix factorization** ($K{=}0$: 0.1562). Sit with that
before rushing past: a sorted list of bestsellers, no learning
whatsoever, outperforms 60,000 trained parameters. On a temporal split
this is not even unusual — late-1990s moviegoers really did watch what
was popular, new releases dominate the future window, and MF's
personalization cannot compensate for never hearing the co-consumption
signal. Every recommender paper that skips the popularity row is hiding
the possibility of exactly this row. **Then the graph pays, layer by
layer**: $K{=}1$ 0.1749, $K{=}2$ 0.1851, $K{=}3$ 0.1953 — each hop of
"users like you" worth roughly two points of recall, monotone, at a
training cost that never exceeds ten seconds on this dataset. The
ladder's shape *is* widget 1's story measured: what popularity gets for
free (global co-consumption) and MF never receives, propagation
delivers in increments.

Note also what the ladder cost: the slowest rung trained in ten
seconds, the whole table — five models, early stopping, evaluation — in
under a minute of GPU. At this dataset's scale, *experiments are free
and the protocol is the scarce resource*: there is no compute excuse
for a missing baseline row or an unmeasured ablation, and when you
graduate to graphs where a rung costs a day, the habits formed where
rungs cost seconds are what keep the expensive table honest. That is
half the pedagogical reason this course runs on small public data; the
other half is that every number above is one you can reproduce tonight.

Two honesty footnotes, both of the kind this course refuses to hide in
appendices. First, NDCG@20 disagrees with Recall@20 about the interior
of the ladder ($K{=}1$ scores 0.1675, a hair above $K{=}3$'s 0.1662,
with $K{=}2$ at 0.1621 between them) — coverage improves monotonically
with depth, placement does not, and a product decision between those
models would hinge on which the surface rewards. When two reasonable
metrics disagree about an ordering, the honest report shows both, and
the suspicious reader asks which one the paper chose to headline.

Second, remember the 66 users: every number in the ladder carries wide
error bars, and the *protocol* conclusions (popularity's strength, the
×1.77) are far more robust than any single third decimal. Small honest
numbers beat large dishonest ones; that ranking never changes.

## The database is a graph: relational deep learning

Return to the marketplace floor — the analytics-ML group replacing
feature pipelines. Their old workflow is the one most of applied ML
still runs: to predict churn, an analyst *joins* users to orders to
payments to tickets, *aggregates* ("orders in last 30 days", "days
since last ticket"), and feeds the resulting flat row to a gradient-
boosted tree. Look at that workflow with Week 14 eyes: the joins walk
foreign keys, the aggregations pool over neighborhoods, the time
windows filter by timestamp. **The analyst is executing a hand-rolled,
frozen, two-layer temporal GNN** — choosing its receptive field, its
aggregators, and its depth by hand, per task, forever.

Walk one prediction to make the claim concrete. Churn, for user 4711,
predicted as of June 1. The analyst's features: `orders_last_30d`
(join users→orders, filter timestamp, count), `avg_ticket_sentiment`
(join users→tickets, aggregate a text score), `favorite_category_share`
(join through orders→items→categories, normalize).

Now the graph view:
user 4711 is a node; its foreign-key edges reach its orders, its
tickets; theirs reach items, agents, categories. A two-layer typed GNN
with time-masked neighborhoods computes, for this node, *learned*
aggregations over exactly those join paths — plus every other
two-hop path the schema affords, including the ones no analyst
proposed, like "tickets about items from categories this user stopped
buying." The feature pipeline is a GNN with its weights chosen by
committee and frozen in a wiki; the GNN is a feature pipeline that
back-propagates. Once seen, the correspondence is hard to unsee — and
the time-masked neighborhood ("use only rows stamped before $t$") is
the database world's beloved *as-of join*, which is to say: this
lecture's temporal wall, discovered independently by every discipline
that ever predicted anything.

Relational Deep Learning names the systematic version of that
replacement, and it deserves the week's last definition.

::: {#def-w14-rdl .definition name="Relational deep learning (RDL)"}
**Relational deep learning** reads a relational database as a temporal
heterogeneous graph — every row a node typed by its table, every
foreign key an edge, every timestamp an event time — and trains a
temporal heterogeneous GNN on it end-to-end, so joins and aggregations
are *learned per task* rather than hand-written per feature. Both
halves are this course's machinery: Week 10's typed message passing,
plus this lecture's time discipline.
:::

A relational database *is* a graph, by construction.
RelBench ([Fey et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.20060)), the
field's benchmark suite, poses exactly the production tasks (churn,
sales forecasts, clinical outcomes) on real multi-table databases,
with — note the reunion — *temporal splits mandated by the benchmark
itself*: every task says "predict at time $t$ using only rows stamped
earlier," because the databases' owners live downstream of the answer.

Early
results follow a pattern you can now predict without reading the
papers: learned models match or beat hand-featured trees on most tasks
while deleting the per-task pipeline work, and the honest caveats live
exactly where this lecture's discipline says to look — entity
resolution, staleness, and whether the tabular baseline got the same
feature budget. The bridge Week 10 built — "your company's most
valuable graph is the one already sitting in Postgres" — is, as of the
mid-2020s, being driven across in production, and it is the single most
likely place a student of this course will apply graph ML without
anyone calling it graph ML.

## Fraud, GraphRAG, and the map

Two shorter placements complete the floor. **Fraud and integrity** is
Week 10 plus Week 14 under adversarial pressure: a heterogeneous graph
(accounts, devices, cards, IPs, addresses) where the signal is
overwhelmingly *relational* — a fraudster can fake any node's features,
but faking a *neighborhood* means acquiring devices, cards, and
histories, which is expensive precisely in proportion to how much the
model reads structure. The sector's signals, in the course's terms:

- **rings** — dense typed subgraphs sharing scarce resources;
- **mule chains** — *ordered* payment paths, money in and out within
  minutes, which is why the snapshot-versus-stream decision from this
  lecture's opening is a fraud team's daily bread;
- **late labels** — ground truth arrives weeks later (chargebacks), so
  models are temporal and evaluation walls are non-negotiable.

What makes the sector intellectually distinct is that
the distribution shift is *directed*: fraudsters A/B test the
detector. Feature-level camouflage adapts in days (aged accounts,
plausible profiles, human-like pacing); structural camouflage adapts
slowly, because it is bought with real resources — which is why
integrity models lean harder on graph signal than any other production
sector, and why their offline metrics decay faster than anyone's. The
honest evaluation here is not even "train past, test future" but
"train past, test future, *assume the future has read your feature
list*" — adversarial validation, the split discipline's final boss.

**GraphRAG** ([Edge et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130))
you already built in Week 5: retrieval
over a curated knowledge graph grounding a language model's answers.
Its Week 14 lesson is operational — the graph is a *product* that
someone must keep fresh, deduplicated, and versioned, and the retrieval
subgraph is a *provenance trail* that makes the system auditable in a
way embedding-only retrieval is not.

The team that owns it spends its
weeks on extraction pipelines (Week 5's information-extraction
plumbing, now with LLMs doing the first pass and humans auditing the
long tail), on entity resolution (the same "is this the same node"
problem RDL hits in customer tables), and on freshness SLAs — when the
refund policy changes at 2 p.m., the graph, not the model, is what
makes the chatbot right by 2:05. It is the sector where this course's
Weeks 4–5 are the whole job description.

Which completes the tour, and earns the map:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w14-map.html >}}

Click your own project's sector and read its "taught in" line — then
click the others anyway, because careers move sideways more often than
job titles admit. The map
is not a list of applications bolted onto a theory course — it is the
syllabus, re-sorted by employer. Recommendation runs on Weeks 3, 6, 11,
and today. Fraud runs on Weeks 2 and 10 with today's clock. Drug
discovery runs on Weeks 7, 9, 12, 13. KG platforms run on Weeks 4 and
5. And the frontier sector — relational deep learning — runs on
precisely the combination (typed graphs, scale discipline, temporal
splits) that the last five weeks assembled. Every sector lists Week 14
because production is not a topic; it is where the topics converge
under one constraint, the clock.

## Common pitfalls

**Random splits on temporal interaction data.** The ×1.77 is not a
worst case — it is a *median* case, and it compounds: model selection
on a leaky split picks the model best at exploiting leakage. If the
data has timestamps, the split uses them; no exceptions survive
contact with this lecture's figure.

**The temporal neighbor sampler that peeks.** "Last 20 interactions
before $t$" implemented as "last 20 interactions" is a one-character
bug ( a missing `< t` filter) that silently hands every temporal model
the future's neighborhoods; nothing crashes, metrics glow, deployment
disappoints. Audit it the way Lab 14's stretch does: query a node at a
timestamp in the middle of its history and assert every returned
neighbor predates it.

**Skipping the popularity baseline.** One line of code stood above
60,000 trained parameters on our honest split. A recommender result
without the popularity row is unfalsifiable in the cheapest possible
way, and reviewers in this field increasingly treat its absence as a
tell.

**Reporting the metric without the candidate set.** Recall@20 against
all 1,682 items is one problem; Recall@20 against 100 sampled
candidates is a much easier one, and mid-2020s audits showed sampled
metrics can even *reorder* systems. Say what was ranked against what,
always.

**Confusing offline metrics with the product.** Recall@K measured on
logged data grades a model against yesterday's behavior — which
yesterday's deployed model shaped (the feedback loop), and which the
new model will change (Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a
target, it stops measuring). Offline numbers select candidates;
only the online A/B grades them. Teams that forget this ship models
that win the replay and lose the quarter.

**Serving stale embeddings.** Precompute-and-serve (the
[@prp-w14-sgc] blessing) has a decay constant: the user who binged a
new genre this morning is still yesterday's vector at noon. Staleness
is a *choice* with a price curve — TGN-style memory, periodic refresh,
or accepting the decay — and the wrong choice is the invisible kind,
because the metric that would expose it is computed offline, where
nothing goes stale.

**Cold start as an afterthought.** Our temporal wall left 877 of 943
users unevaluable — and a real system meets those users every hour.
Pure ID embeddings have literally nothing to say about a node with no
edges; production systems bolt on content features, two-tower
encoders, or popularity fallbacks. If your evaluation quietly drops
cold nodes (ours did, and said so), your headline number describes
only the warm world.

## Required reading

- **[He et al. — LightGCN: Simplifying and Powering Graph Convolution
  Network for Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.02126)**
  (SIGIR 2020). Read §2 for the deletion
  experiments (what happens as each GCN part is removed) and notice the
  ablation discipline — the paper *earns* its simplicity claim
  empirically, which is why it aged well.
- **[Rossi et al. — Temporal Graph Networks for Deep Learning on Dynamic
  Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10637)** (2020). The memory /
  message / embedding decomposition of
  §3 is the architecture-level understanding this lecture requires; the
  staleness discussion around the embedding module is the part
  practitioners quote.

Optional: [Ying et al., *PinSage*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01973)
(KDD 2018) — read it as a systems
paper and count the Week 11 techniques; [Fey et al., *RelBench /
Relational Deep Learning*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.20060) (2024) —
the database-as-graph position paper,
with the temporal-split mandate worth imitating everywhere; the
[Temporal Graph Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01026) line of
work, for the same protocol
standardization applied to TGN-style models (its headline finding —
rankings scramble when evaluation gets harder negatives and real
temporal splits — should sound familiar five sections after our own
table); and [Ferrari Dacrema et al., *Are We Really Making Much
Progress?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06902) (RecSys 2019) — the
audit that found simple, well-tuned
baselines beating a decade of neural recommenders under honest
protocols. Read that last one the way this course has taught you to:
not as cynicism about neural methods, but as a demonstration that the
field's tables were measuring tuning effort and protocol looseness —
and that whoever controls the baseline controls the conclusion. It is
this lecture's evaluation sermon delivered as a crime report, and it
is why our own ladder carries a popularity row.

## Check your understanding

**Q1.** Derive LightGCN from GCN: name the three deletions and give the
one-sentence justification for each on ID-featured bipartite graphs.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Delete the weight matrices $W$ (inputs are free embeddings — any
useful linear remix can be absorbed into the embeddings themselves, so
$W$ only adds parameters and optimization surface); delete the
nonlinearity (between averaging steps it mostly destroys sign/magnitude
information that dot-product scoring needs, and ablations show it
hurts); delete the self-loop, replacing it with the layer-mean readout
(the $k{=}0$ term keeps every node's own embedding in the final answer,
while averaging tempers oversmoothing).
</details>

**Q2.** Your colleague's MF recommender reports Recall@20 = 0.34 on
MovieLens with a random split. Using this lecture's measurements, what
do you predict happens to that number under a global temporal split,
and what *specifically* leaks under the random one?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Expect roughly a 40–45% drop (our K=3 fell 0.346 → 0.195, ×1.77). The
leak: with interactions hidden uniformly in time, most users have
training interactions that *postdate* their test interactions, so the
model learns future co-consumption patterns (and future item
popularity) to "predict" the past. Deployment never gets that gift —
it extrapolates forward only.
</details>

**Q3.** Popularity beat BPR-MF on our temporal split (0.1655 vs
0.1562) yet lost to it under leave-last-out (0.1266 vs 0.2096). Explain
both directions in the course's vocabulary.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
The temporal test window is dominated by what was globally popular
*in that future period* (new releases), which the popularity ranker
tracks for free while MF — barred from the co-consumption signal —
cannot personalize its way past it with only past data. Leave-last-out
evaluates one item per user scattered across the whole timeline, so
global future popularity matters less and personalization pays;
also its 940-user population versus temporal's 66 changes what is even
being averaged. Same models — the protocols ask different questions.
</details>

**Q4.** State [@prp-w14-sgc] and give its two production consequences.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
LightGCN's encoder is $E = \frac{1}{K+1}\sum_k \hat A^k E^{(0)}$ — a
fixed polynomial in the normalized adjacency applied to the trained
embedding table; it is SGC with identity features. Consequences:
serving is precompute-and-dot-product (all graph work done offline,
Week 11's discipline), and the expressiveness ceiling of a fixed linear
filter applies — plus the corollary cost of precomputation: staleness,
which must be managed as an explicit choice.
</details>

**Q5.** A payments fraud team debates snapshots-per-hour versus an
event-stream model. Give one concrete fraud pattern that decides the
question, and say which Week 14 architecture component captures it.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Mule-chain forwarding: money enters an account and leaves it minutes
later, repeatedly along a path. Hourly snapshots collapse each hop's
*order* — in-edge and out-edge coexist with no sequence — so the
defining signal vanishes. An event-stream model's per-node memory
(TGN's GRU state) updates on the incoming transfer *before* the
outgoing one arrives, so the order is encoded in the state trajectory.
</details>

**Q6.** Compute by hand: ranked list of 10, relevant items at ranks 2
and 6, $|P| = 2$. Recall@5 and NDCG@5?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Top 5 contains the rank-2 hit only: Recall@5 = 1/min(2,5) = **0.5**.
DCG@5 = $1/\log_2 3 = 0.631$; IDCG@5 = $1/\log_2 2 + 1/\log_2 3 =
1.631$; NDCG@5 = $0.631/1.631 = \mathbf{0.387}$.
</details>

**Q7.** Why does RelBench *mandate* temporal splits rather than merely
recommending them, and what does the analyst-with-joins comparison
predict about where learned models win most?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Database tasks are forecasting tasks by nature — "will this customer
churn" is only meaningful with information up to a cutoff — so a random
split would let the model read post-outcome rows (support tickets filed
*after* the churn) and produce numbers unrelated to deployment; the
mandate makes the leak impossible rather than discouraged. The
comparison predicts learned models win most where useful signal lies in
joins the analyst didn't think to write — deep, multi-hop, or
cross-table interactions beyond the standard feature recipes — and win
least where decades of feature craft already encode the graph walk.
</details>

**Q8.** Your project's offline Recall@20 improved 8% over the deployed
model. Name the two reasons this does not yet justify shipping, and the
mechanism behind each.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Feedback loop: the logged data was generated under the old model's
exposure choices, so offline replay grades the new model on the old
model's world — items the new model would surface were rarely shown,
hence rarely logged as positives (the improvement may be
under- or over-stated). Goodhart: deployment changes user behavior
itself, and a model optimized hard against the offline proxy can win
the proxy while degrading the product (clickbait-shaped ranking). Both
are resolved only by an online A/B — offline metrics nominate, the
experiment decides.
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **temporal event stream** (@def-w14-stream) — the graph as a history:
  timestamped edges arriving forever.
- **TGN memory / message / embedding** (@eq-w14-tgn, @eq-w14-tgn-embed)
  — per-node state, GRU-updated per event, read out time-aware.
- **layer-mean readout** (@eq-w14-readout) — LightGCN's replacement for
  the self-loop: average all depths, keeping the $k{=}0$ voice.
- **BPR** (@def-w14-bpr) — pairwise ranking loss: observed item over
  sampled unobserved item.
- **Recall@K / NDCG@K** (@def-w14-metrics) — coverage vs. placement at
  ranking cutoff $K$.
- **global temporal split** (@def-w14-wall) — a hard wall at one
  timestamp, certified by a single assert; deployment's contract.
- **relational deep learning** (@def-w14-rdl) — the database as a
  temporal heterogeneous graph; joins and aggregations, learned.
- **two-stage serving** — ANN retrieval over precomputed embeddings,
  then a heavy ranker.
- **popularity baseline** — the one-line ranker whose absence from a
  results table is a tell.
:::

## Where this leaves us

The last machinery lecture of the course closes its oldest loop. Week 1
promised that graphs were a way of seeing systems; Week 14 showed the
systems that pay for the seeing. The models today were deliberately
modest — a lookup table with a memory, a GCN with everything deleted —
and that modesty is the finding: at production scale, with the clock
running, the winning moves are Week 11's precomputation, Week 12's
split discipline, Week 4's ranking losses, Week 2's baselines. The
sophistication lives in the *protocol*, which is exactly where this
course has been putting it all semester.

It is also worth saying what this week's measured table adds to the
course's growing shelf of honest verdicts, because the shelf now reads
as one argument. Week 10: a frozen lookup matched a trained encoder —
architecture is not automatically signal. Week 11: a random partition
survived on 2.5% of the edges — scale bends but rarely breaks the
simple thing. Week 12: a leak scored *below* random — protocols fail
loudly if you build them to. Week 13: the encoding paid and the
attention didn't, at one budget — ingredients must be priced
separately. Week 14: the split alone moved the number ×1.77, and a
sorted list beat a trained model — the protocol *is* the result.

Five
tables, one thesis: in this field, at this moment, careful measurement
is the scarcest skill — scarcer than architectural novelty, and, on
the evidence of your own notebooks, entirely learnable.

Close the loop — one minute, no notes: the three GCN deletions and why
each is safe on ID features; the co-consumption hop's mass at $K{=}2$
on the widget graph; the three protocol numbers and which one
deployment signs; popularity's number and what it humbled; TGN's three
components and the one-batch-late trick that keeps them honest. If any
of the five stalls, its section is a four-minute reread tonight and a
zero-minute regret on Thursday. Then do the transfer test that decides
whether this week actually landed: pick any system you use daily — a
feed, a map, a fraud check at checkout — and narrate its graph, its
clock, its split, and its probable baseline. If you can, you have the
week; if a step stalls, you have found tonight's rereading.

Because next Thursday is the final exam — cumulative, with its center
of mass on Weeks 9–14, one A4 sheet of your own notes allowed. The best
revision artifact you own is widget 4: pick each sector, and for each
"taught in" week, reconstruct that week's one measured table and its
one-sentence verdict. The course taught perhaps two dozen numbers
